```{r helpers, echo=FALSE}
# scientific workflow schematic; 'highlight' shades one box
draw_workflow <- function(highlight = NULL, cex = 0.9) {
  boxes <- c("PROBLEM", "THEORIES", "MODELS", "FIT", "COMPARE")
  subs <- c("what do we\nneed to know?", "candidate\nexplanations",
            "data-generating\n(process + noise)", "confront each\nwith data",
            "fit, prediction,\nrelevance")
  x <- seq(1, 9, by = 2)
  y <- 2
  w <- 0.8
  h <- 0.55
  shade <- function(lab) if (!is.null(highlight) && lab == highlight) "lightskyblue1" else "white"
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(-0.2, 4), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_along(boxes)) {
    rect(x[i] - w, y - h, x[i] + w, y + h, col = shade(boxes[i]), lwd = 1.5)
    text(x[i], y + 0.18, boxes[i], font = 2, cex = cex)
    text(x[i], y - 0.22, subs[i], cex = cex * 0.75)
  }
  arrows(x[-5] + w, y, x[-1] - w, y, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  rect(6 - 0.7, 3.2 - 0.35, 6 + 0.7, 3.2 + 0.35, lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  text(6, 3.28, "DATA", font = 2, cex = cex)
  text(6, 3.0, "study design", cex = cex * 0.75)
  arrows(x[3], y + h, 6 - 0.7, 3.2, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  arrows(6 + 0.7, 3.2, x[4], y + h, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  segments(x[5], y - h, x[5], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  segments(x[5], 0.4, x[1], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  arrows(x[c(1, 2)], 0.4, x[c(1, 2)], y - h, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  text(6, 0.15, "REVISE the problem and theories; drop or down-weight poor models",
       cex = cex * 0.85, font = 3)
}
```

Packages: `emdbook`, `cmdstanr`. Reading: Bolker 6.6.5 (model
criticism and goodness-of-fit tests).

# What makes a model good? {#good}

Model comparison ranks a set of candidate models, but the best of a
bad set is still a bad model. This page asks whether a fitted model is
any good: could it have produced the data, does it predict data it
hasn't seen, and does it hold up outside the range of the data used to
fit it?

## 1. Big picture

```{r workflow, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.8, dev="png", dpi=250}
draw_workflow("COMPARE")
```

The COMPARE step asks three things of a model: does it fit the data,
does it predict better than its rivals (including a null model), and is
it relevant to the problem? [Model comparison](Week10_ModelComparison.html)
covers the rivals. Here the focus is on a single fitted model, and
"good" can mean any of these:

1. **Goodness of fit** (adequacy): the observed data could reasonably
   have been generated by the fitted model.
2. **Predictive performance** (usefulness): the model predicts new
   observations well, not just the ones used to fit it.
3. **Generality**: the model still predicts well outside the range of
   the data used to fit it (extrapolation).

For causal questions, a model can be good without predicting well: what
matters is whether it estimates the effect of A on B without bias, which
depends on which variables it includes (see
[causal diagrams](Week10_ModelComparison.html#dags)).

## 2. Example: myxomatosis titers {#myxo}

Bolker's myxomatosis data give virus titers in rabbits infected with
grade 1 virus, measured 2 to 9 days after infection. Titer rises and
then falls, so a Ricker function $\mu = a\,t\,e^{-bt}$ describes the
mean, with Gamma noise (shape $s$, scale $\mu/s$, so the mean is $\mu$):

```{r myxo-fit}
library(emdbook)
myx <- subset(MyxoTiter_sum, grade == 1)   # 27 rabbits

ricker <- function(a, b, t) a * t * exp(-b * t)

# Gamma NLL with Ricker mean; 'd' lets us refit to subsets later
nll_myx <- function(p, d = myx) {
  if (any(p <= 0)) return(Inf)
  mu <- ricker(p[1], p[2], d$day)
  -sum(dgamma(d$titer, shape = p[3], scale = mu / p[3], log = TRUE))
}

fit <- optim(c(a = 1, b = 0.2, shape = 50), nll_myx)
mle <- fit$par
round(mle, 3)
```

The MLE is $a$ = `r f2(mle["a"])`, $b$ = `r f3(mle["b"])`, shape
`r f1(mle["shape"])` (NLL `r f2(fit$value)`).

# Goodness of fit {#gof}

A model fits if data simulated from it look like the real data. The
simplest checks plot the range of data the fitted model expects; more
formal ones compare a summary statistic of the real data with the same
statistic computed on many simulated data sets.

## 1. Plug-in prediction bounds

Plug the MLE into the Gamma distribution and take its 2.5% and 97.5%
quantiles on each day. About 95% of observations should fall between
them:

```{r plugin, fig.height=4}
days <- seq(1, 10, by = 0.1)
mu_days <- ricker(mle["a"], mle["b"], days)
upper <- qgamma(0.975, shape = mle["shape"], scale = mu_days / mle["shape"])
lower <- qgamma(0.025, shape = mle["shape"], scale = mu_days / mle["shape"])

par(mar = c(4, 4, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(titer ~ day, data = myx, pch = 16, xlim = c(1, 10), ylim = c(0, 12),
     xlab = "Days since infection", ylab = "Titer")
lines(days, mu_days, lwd = 2)
lines(days, upper, lty = 2)
lines(days, lower, lty = 2)
```

```{r plugin-count, echo=FALSE}
mu_obs <- ricker(mle["a"], mle["b"], myx$day)
inside <- with(myx, titer > qgamma(0.025, shape = mle["shape"], scale = mu_obs / mle["shape"]) &
                    titer < qgamma(0.975, shape = mle["shape"], scale = mu_obs / mle["shape"]))
```

`r sum(inside)` of the 27 titers fall inside the bounds.

## 2. Parametric bootstrap {#parametric-bootstrap}

The same idea by simulation: generate many data sets of 27 rabbits
from the fitted model, on the observed days, and compare. Simulating
from a fitted model is called a **parametric bootstrap**.

> **Question:** How does a parametric bootstrap differ from the
> [ordinary (nonparametric) bootstrap](Week1_IntroAndAlgorithms.html#bootstrap)?
> What does each assume?

A plot shows *where* a model misses. A test statistic (a single number
summarizing the data) asks whether the misses are bigger than the
model's own noise would produce. Here the statistic is the root mean
squared error (RMSE) around the fitted mean:

```{r param-boot, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.8}
mu_obs <- ricker(mle["a"], mle["b"], myx$day)
rmse <- function(y, mu) sqrt(mean((y - mu)^2))

set.seed(746)
sims <- replicate(1000, rgamma(nrow(myx), shape = mle["shape"], scale = mu_obs / mle["shape"]))
rmse_sim <- apply(sims, 2, rmse, mu = mu_obs)
rmse_obs <- rmse(myx$titer, mu_obs)
p_boot <- mean(rmse_sim >= rmse_obs)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 0.5, 0.5))
boxplot(c(sims) ~ rep(myx$day, times = 1000), at = sort(unique(myx$day)),
        xlim = c(1.5, 9.5), ylim = c(0, 12), col = "grey90", range = 0,
        xlab = "Days since infection", ylab = "Titer")
points(titer ~ day, data = myx, pch = 16, col = "firebrick")
hist(rmse_sim, breaks = 30, col = "grey80", border = "white", main = "",
     xlab = "RMSE of a simulated data set")
abline(v = rmse_obs, lwd = 3, col = "firebrick")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The observed RMSE, `r f2(rmse_obs)`, sits in the middle of the
simulated ones: `r f2(p_boot)` of the simulated data sets have a larger
RMSE. By this check the scatter around the curve is what the model
expects. A different statistic could still expose a problem: the range,
the largest residual, or the residuals' trend with day. Choose
statistics that target what matters for the problem, and that the fit
doesn't force to match automatically (the mean titer, for example,
almost always matches). The tree example in
[simulating data](Week5_SimulatingData.html#gof) shows a model that
fails this kind of check.

Both checks above treat the MLE as the true parameter values. Adding
parameter uncertainty within maximum likelihood takes extra work:
propagating the confidence intervals (for example by the
[delta method](lecture_notes/NOTES_Reference_DeltaMethod.pdf)), or
simulating from a range of parameter values (which a strict frequentist
would object to, since parameters aren't random in that framework). In
a Bayesian fit it comes for free.

## 3. Posterior predictive checks {#ppc}

A **posterior predictive check** simulates new data sets, the same size
and with the same covariates as the real one, from many draws of the
posterior. Each simulated data set uses a different parameter draw, so
parameter uncertainty is built in.

```{r myxo-stan, cache=TRUE, results="hide"}
library(cmdstanr)
ricker_code <- "
data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  vector<lower=0>[N] day;
  vector<lower=0>[N] titer;
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0> a;
  real<lower=0> b;
  real<lower=0> shape;
}
model {
  vector[N] mu = a * day .* exp(-b * day);
  titer ~ gamma(shape, shape ./ mu);   // rate = shape / mean
}
"
ricker_model <- cmdstan_model(write_stan_file(ricker_code))
fit_stan <- ricker_model$sample(
  data = list(N = nrow(myx), day = myx$day, titer = myx$titer),
  chains = 4, parallel_chains = 4, seed = 746
)
post <- as.data.frame(posterior::as_draws_df(fit_stan$draws(c("a", "b", "shape"))))
```

With no prior statements, `a`, `b`, and `shape` get flat priors on the
positive values. For each of 1,000 posterior draws, compute the mean at
each observed day, simulate 27 titers, and compute the RMSE of both the
real and the simulated titers around that draw's mean:

```{r ppc, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.8}
set.seed(746)
use <- sample(nrow(post), 1000)
ppc <- t(sapply(use, function(i) {
  mu <- ricker(post$a[i], post$b[i], myx$day)
  y_rep <- rgamma(nrow(myx), shape = post$shape[i], scale = mu / post$shape[i])
  c(obs = rmse(myx$titer, mu), rep = rmse(y_rep, mu))
}))
p_bayes <- mean(ppc[, "rep"] >= ppc[, "obs"])

# posterior predictive 95% band across days: 10 simulated titers per draw and day
band <- sapply(days, function(t) {
  mu <- rep(ricker(post$a, post$b, t), 10)
  shape <- rep(post$shape, 10)
  quantile(rgamma(length(mu), shape = shape, scale = mu / shape), c(0.025, 0.975))
})

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(titer ~ day, data = myx, pch = 16, xlim = c(1, 10), ylim = c(0, 12),
     xlab = "Days since infection", ylab = "Titer")
polygon(c(days, rev(days)), c(band[1, ], rev(band[2, ])), col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.25),
        border = NA)
lines(days, ricker(median(post$a), median(post$b), days), lwd = 2)
plot(ppc[, "obs"], ppc[, "rep"], pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = adjustcolor("black", 0.4),
     xlim = range(ppc), ylim = range(ppc), xlab = "RMSE, real data", ylab = "RMSE, simulated data")
abline(0, 1, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The share of points above the 1:1 line is the **posterior predictive
p-value**, here `r f2(p_bayes)`. Values near 0 or 1 flag a
discrepancy: the real data are farther from (near 0) or closer to (near
1) the model's predictions than its own simulated data would be. The
band is slightly wider than the plug-in bounds because it includes
parameter uncertainty.

# Predictive performance {#prediction}

A model can fit well and still be of little use if it explains only a
small share of the variation. And a model that fits too well, by
fitting the noise, predicts new data badly. This part measures
predictive skill on the data used to fit, on new data, and by
cross-validation.

## 1. Measures of skill {#skill}

- $R^2 = 1 - \text{SS}_\text{res}/\text{SS}_\text{tot}$: the share of
  the variance around the mean that the model explains.
- **McFadden's pseudo-$R^2$** $= 1 - \ell_\text{model}/\ell_\text{null}$,
  where $\ell$ is the maximized log-likelihood and the null model has a
  constant mean. It works on the likelihood scale, so it suits any error
  distribution. (It assumes both log-likelihoods are negative, which is
  always true for discrete data.)
- **Root mean squared error**, $\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\text{mean}(\text{residual}^2)}$,
  in the units of the response: "the model is usually within about
  `r f1(rmse_obs)` titer units."

```{r skill}
nll_null <- function(p) {
  if (any(p <= 0)) return(Inf)
  -sum(dgamma(myx$titer, shape = p[2], scale = p[1] / p[2], log = TRUE))
}
fit_null <- optim(c(mean = 7, shape = 10), nll_null)

r2 <- 1 - sum((myx$titer - mu_obs)^2) / sum((myx$titer - mean(myx$titer))^2)
mcfadden <- 1 - fit$value / fit_null$value     # NLLs: the minus signs cancel
round(c(R2 = r2, McFadden = mcfadden, RMSE = rmse_obs), 3)
```

> **Question:** Picture an overfit model, such as a curve through every
> point. Would it pass the goodness-of-fit checks above? How would its
> $R^2$ and RMSE look? How well would it predict new rabbits?

## 2. Validation with new data {#validation}

The most direct test of prediction is new data that played no part in
fitting. Suppose a second study measures seven more grade 1 rabbits, on
days 2 to 8:

```{r validation-data}
new1 <- data.frame(day = 2:8, titer = c(4.4, 7.2, 6.8, 5.9, 9.1, 8.3, 8.8))
```

```{r validation-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4}
days20 <- seq(1, 17, by = 0.1)
mu20 <- ricker(mle["a"], mle["b"], days20)
plot_bounds <- function(xlim) {
  par(mar = c(4, 4, 0.5, 0.5))
  plot(titer ~ day, data = myx, pch = 16, xlim = xlim, ylim = c(0, 12),
       xlab = "Days since infection", ylab = "Titer")
  lines(days20, mu20, lwd = 2)
  lines(days20, qgamma(0.975, shape = mle["shape"], scale = mu20 / mle["shape"]), lty = 2)
  lines(days20, qgamma(0.025, shape = mle["shape"], scale = mu20 / mle["shape"]), lty = 2)
}
plot_bounds(c(1, 10))
points(titer ~ day, data = new1, pch = 17, cex = 1.3, col = "firebrick")
legend("topleft", c("data used to fit", "new data"), pch = c(16, 17),
       col = c("black", "firebrick"), bty = "n")
```

Score the predictions with the same three measures. For new data, the
log-likelihoods use the parameters fitted to the original rabbits:

```{r validation}
skill <- function(d) {
  mu <- ricker(mle["a"], mle["b"], d$day)
  ll_model <- sum(dgamma(d$titer, shape = mle["shape"], scale = mu / mle["shape"], log = TRUE))
  ll_null <- sum(dgamma(d$titer, shape = fit_null$par["shape"],
                        scale = fit_null$par["mean"] / fit_null$par["shape"], log = TRUE))
  c(R2 = 1 - sum((d$titer - mu)^2) / sum((d$titer - mean(d$titer))^2),
    McFadden = 1 - ll_model / ll_null,
    RMSE = rmse(d$titer, mu))
}
skill_new1 <- skill(new1)
round(skill_new1, 3)
```

The model still explains about as much of the variation
($R^2$ = `r f2(skill_new1["R2"])`), though the typical error grows from
`r f2(rmse_obs)` to `r f2(skill_new1["RMSE"])`.

## 3. Extrapolation {#extrapolation}

Now suppose the second study followed rabbits from day 10 to day 16,
past the end of the original data:

```{r extrapolation, fig.height=4}
new2 <- data.frame(day = 10:16, titer = c(6.8, 8.0, 4.5, 3.1, 2.7, 1.2, 0.04))
skill_new2 <- skill(new2)
round(skill_new2, 3)
```

```{r extrapolation-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4}
plot_bounds(c(1, 17))
points(titer ~ day, data = new2, pch = 17, cex = 1.3, col = "firebrick")
legend("topright", c("data used to fit", "new data, days 10-16"), pch = c(16, 17),
       col = c("black", "firebrick"), bty = "n")
```

The Ricker curve has the right general shape, so $R^2$ is still
positive (`r f2(skill_new2["R2"])`). But the titers fall faster than
the model expects, and the narrow Gamma noise makes those misses very
unlikely under the model. The pseudo-$R^2$ is negative
(`r f2(skill_new2["McFadden"])`): on the likelihood scale the model
does worse than a constant mean. Some lessons:

- Models are often poor at extrapolation.
- $R^2$ isn't always the best measure of performance; it ignores the
  noise part of the model.
- Out-of-sample pseudo-$R^2$ can be negative.
- Check goodness of fit as well as predictive skill.

## 4. Cross-validation {#cross-validation}

New data are often unavailable. Cross-validation holds out part of the
data instead:

1. Split the data into $k$ groups (**folds**).
2. For each fold: fit the model to all the other folds, then predict the
   held-out fold.
3. Score all the held-out predictions together.

Ten folds is a common choice ($k$-fold cross-validation, used to choose
the penalty in [regularization](Week10_ModelComparison.html#lab-tools)).
With $k = n$, each observation is held out once: **leave-one-out**
cross-validation (also called the jackknife). With 27 rabbits,
leave-one-out means 27 refits:

```{r loo-cv}
pred_cv <- numeric(nrow(myx))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(myx))) {
  fit_i <- optim(mle, nll_myx, d = myx[-i, ])        # fit without rabbit i
  pred_cv[i] <- ricker(fit_i$par["a"], fit_i$par["b"], myx$day[i])   # predict rabbit i
}

var_explained <- function(pred) 1 - mean((myx$titer - pred)^2) / mean((myx$titer - mean(myx$titer))^2)
round(rbind(all_data = c(RMSE = rmse(myx$titer, mu_obs), var_explained = var_explained(mu_obs)),
            cross_validation = c(rmse(myx$titer, pred_cv), var_explained(pred_cv))), 3)
```

Performance under cross-validation is lower, and almost always will be,
but it is a more honest estimate of how the model would do on new
rabbits.

The gap between the two grows with model flexibility. In the widget, 20
points come from a hump-shaped curve plus noise. Raise the degree of the
polynomial fitted to them and compare the error on the data used to fit
with the leave-one-out error:

```{r cv-widget, echo=FALSE}
widget("cv_overfit.html")
```

> **Question:** Which degree gives the lowest cross-validation error?
> What happens to the two errors above that degree, and why does the
> error on the fitting data never go up? Click "New sample" a few times:
> does the best degree stay the same?

# Binary responses: ROC curves and AUC {#roc}

For a 0/1 response, RMSE and $R^2$ say little: every observation is 0
or 1, and the predictions are probabilities. This part scores a
logistic regression by how well it ranks occupied sites above
unoccupied ones, with and without cross-validation.

## 1. Example: pika occupancy {#pikas}

Simulated data: surveys of 120 talus patches record whether pikas are
present. Occupancy rises with elevation (cooler) and patch area. Two
models: a habitat model with elevation and log area, and the same model
plus eight measured covariates that, unknown to the analyst, have
nothing to do with pikas.

```{r pika-data}
set.seed(746)
n <- 120
patches <- data.frame(elev = round(runif(n, 2400, 3400)),
                      area = round(exp(rnorm(n, log(0.8), 0.9)), 2))
for (j in 1:8) patches[[paste0("x", j)]] <- rnorm(n)    # irrelevant covariates
eta <- -0.3 + 1.3 * (patches$elev - 2900) / 300 + 0.8 * (log(patches$area) - log(0.8)) / 0.9
patches$occupied <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(eta))

f_habitat <- occupied ~ scale(elev) + scale(log(area))
f_big <- update(f_habitat, paste(". ~ . +", paste0("x", 1:8, collapse = " + ")))
m_habitat <- glm(f_habitat, family = binomial, data = patches)
m_big <- glm(f_big, family = binomial, data = patches)
```

`r sum(patches$occupied)` of the 120 patches are occupied. Ten-fold
cross-validation gives each patch a predicted probability from a model
that never saw it:

```{r pika-cv}
folds <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = n))
cv_predict <- function(formula) {
  p <- numeric(n)
  for (k in 1:10) {
    m <- glm(formula, family = binomial, data = patches[folds != k, ])
    p[folds == k] <- predict(m, patches[folds == k, ], type = "response")
  }
  p
}
p_cv_habitat <- cv_predict(f_habitat)
p_cv_big <- cv_predict(f_big)
```

## 2. Thresholds and the ROC curve {#roc-curve}

To turn a predicted probability into "occupied" or "not," pick a
threshold: call every patch above it occupied. Then count:

- **true positive rate** (sensitivity): the share of occupied patches
  called occupied;
- **false positive rate** (1 minus specificity): the share of
  unoccupied patches called occupied.

Any single threshold is arbitrary. A threshold of 0 calls every patch
occupied (both rates are 1); a threshold of 1 calls none occupied (both
rates are 0). The **receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve**
traces both rates over every threshold in between, so it doesn't depend
on any one choice.

In the widget, the model gives each site a score; the two curves show
the scores of unoccupied and occupied sites. Move the threshold, then
change how well the scores separate the two groups:

```{r roc-widget, echo=FALSE}
widget("roc_threshold.html")
```

> **Question:** What does the ROC curve look like for a perfect
> classifier? For one no better than flipping a coin? For one worse than
> a coin, and how would you fix that model?

## 3. Area under the curve {#auc}

The **area under the ROC curve (AUC)** summarizes it in one number: 1
for perfect ranking, 0.5 for a coin flip. It equals the probability
that a randomly chosen occupied patch gets a higher predicted
probability than a randomly chosen unoccupied one, which gives a short
way to compute it from ranks:

```{r auc}
auc <- function(p, y) {
  r <- rank(p)
  n1 <- sum(y)
  n0 <- sum(1 - y)
  (sum(r[y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}

# ROC curve: true and false positive rates over every threshold
roc_points <- function(p, y) {
  thr <- c(Inf, sort(unique(p), decreasing = TRUE))
  cbind(fpr = sapply(thr, function(t) mean(p[y == 0] >= t)),
        tpr = sapply(thr, function(t) mean(p[y == 1] >= t)))
}
```

```{r auc-table}
y <- patches$occupied
dev <- function(p) -2 * sum(dbinom(y, 1, p, log = TRUE))
dev_null <- dev(rep(mean(y), n))
perf <- rbind(
  habitat_all_data = c(AUC = auc(fitted(m_habitat), y), McFadden = 1 - dev(fitted(m_habitat)) / dev_null),
  habitat_cv       = c(auc(p_cv_habitat, y), 1 - dev(p_cv_habitat) / dev_null),
  big_all_data     = c(auc(fitted(m_big), y), 1 - dev(fitted(m_big)) / dev_null),
  big_cv           = c(auc(p_cv_big, y), 1 - dev(p_cv_big) / dev_null)
)
round(perf, 3)
```

```{r roc-plot, fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(roc_points(fitted(m_big), y), type = "s", lwd = 2, col = "grey60",
     xlab = "False positive rate", ylab = "True positive rate")
lines(roc_points(p_cv_big, y), type = "s", lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "grey60")
lines(roc_points(p_cv_habitat, y), type = "s", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue")
abline(0, 1, lty = 3)
legend("bottomright", c("big model, all data", "big model, cross-validated",
                        "habitat model, cross-validated"),
       lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2, 1), col = c("grey60", "grey60", "steelblue"), bty = "n")
```

On the data used to fit, the big model looks better: AUC
`r f2(perf["big_all_data", "AUC"])` vs. `r f2(perf["habitat_all_data", "AUC"])`.
Under cross-validation the order flips
(`r f2(perf["big_cv", "AUC"])` vs. `r f2(perf["habitat_cv", "AUC"])`),
and the big model's pseudo-$R^2$ drops from
`r f2(perf["big_all_data", "McFadden"])` to `r f2(perf["big_cv", "McFadden"])`.
The eight extra covariates fit noise in the patches used to fit the
model, and that noise doesn't carry over to new patches.

## Discussion {#discussion}

1. The myxomatosis model passes the parametric bootstrap check
   (p = `r f2(p_boot)`) and explains `r round(100 * r2)`% of the
   variance in the data used to fit it, but its pseudo-$R^2$ on days 10
   to 16 is `r f2(skill_new2["McFadden"])`. Is it a good model? Good
   for what?
2. Leave-one-out and 10-fold cross-validation can give different
   answers. Leave-one-out uses almost all the data for each fit; what
   might that cost? Think about rabbits measured on the same day, or
   pika patches on the same slope.
3. A pika occupancy model with a cross-validated AUC of
   `r f2(perf["habitat_cv", "AUC"])` will guide where to survey next
   year. A manager asks for a single threshold to call a patch
   "occupied." What would you need to know to choose it?
